questions.question: Describe the four things a tender board listens for in a presentation and explain why evidence matters more than claims.
questions.expected_answer: Whether the team understands the problem and the users, shown by site measurements and user needs; whether the design meets the specifications, shown by the drawing and model with gradient, risers, landings and rails checkable; whether the price is realistic and traceable, shown by the budget page and the ability to explain any line; and whether the team can be trusted to build it, shown by the quality of drawings and model, safe methods and honest answers. Evidence matters because the board must spend the client's money and can only compare bids on what can be checked; a claim such as very safe cannot be compared, while 1 in 12 with 1 200 landings and rails at 900 shown on the plan can.

questions.question: Set out the structure and timing of a tender presentation for the stairs and ramp and explain how the speaking is shared and rehearsed.
questions.expected_answer: Opening half a minute: team, problem and solution in a sentence each. Investigate one minute: site, users, lessons from existing entrances. Design two minutes: brief, two ideas, the scorecard and the choice, the working drawing with key dimensions. Make one minute: the model, how it was built to the drawing and checked. Budget one minute: section totals, grand total, inclusions, exclusions, price date. Close half a minute: two or three reasons to choose the bid. Each member presents one stage and knows the others well enough to help, handovers are quick, visual aids are the sketches, drawing, budget page and model, and the team rehearses against a timer, cuts to fit, and prepares answers to predicted questions from the file.

questions.question: Explain how a team should answer the board's questions and how a learner on the board should score other teams' bids.
questions.expected_answer: Answer briefly with evidence, pointing to the dimension on the drawing or the quantity and source in the budget; let the member who knows best answer without talking over others; admit honestly when something is not known and say how it would be found out, rather than bluffing; accept valid criticism and show where the file answers a misreading. On the board, score each bid on a sheet built from the design considerations and specifications, understanding, specifications met, drawings, model, budget, presentation and answers, writing a short reason for each score during and immediately after the presentation, scoring the bid and not the people.
